statement: Omar is planning a rectangular vegetable garden whose length is $3$ meters more than twice its width. He has at most $72$ meters of fencing to go around the whole garden, and he wants the length to be at least $15$ meters. If the width must be a whole number of meters, how many different widths are possible?

choices.misconception: I found the width can go from $6$ to $11$ and subtracted $11 - 6$, which leaves out one of the endpoints.
I only used the fencing limit, $w \le 11$, and counted the widths $1$ through $11$, forgetting the length must be at least $15$.
I used length plus width for the fencing instead of the full perimeter, so $3w + 3 \le 72$ gave $w \le 23$ and I counted $6$ through $23$.

hints: Write the length in terms of the width $w$, then turn each condition into an inequality in $w$.
The length is $2w + 3$. The fencing condition uses the perimeter, $2(w + 2w + 3) \le 72$, and the length condition is $2w + 3 \ge 15$.
The perimeter condition gives $6w + 6 \le 72$, so $w \le 11$. The length condition gives $w \ge 6$. Count the whole numbers from $6$ to $11$ inclusive.

solutions.reliable: Let the width be $w$, so the length is $2w + 3$. Fencing: $2(w + 2w + 3) = 6w + 6 \le 72$, so $w \le 11$. Length: $2w + 3 \ge 15$, so $w \ge 6$. The whole numbers with $6 \le w \le 11$ are $6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11$, which is $6$ widths. Check the ends: $w = 6$ gives length $15$ and perimeter $42$; $w = 11$ gives length $25$ and perimeter $72$.
solutions.elegant: The number of whole numbers from $a$ to $b$ inclusive is $b - a + 1$, here $11 - 6 + 1 = 6$.
